passage.title: Keeper of the Glass Rings
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
In the autumn of 1898, twelve-year-old Caleb climbed the spiral iron steps of the St. Simons Island Lighthouse. Outside the thick brick tower, gray clouds rolled low across the Georgia sound. Stiff gusts of wind rattled the brass window latches and drove white foam across the marsh grass. Caleb's father had ridden into the village to fetch clean lamp oil before the gale struck. Before leaving, he had trusted Caleb with the afternoon chore that mattered most to passing ships.

At the top of the stairs, Caleb stepped into the bright lantern room. Directly in the center stood the great Fresnel lens, shaped like a giant beehive of polished glass rings and brass frames. Even a thin film of soot from last night's oil wick or a smudge of salt dust could dim the beacon's reach across the dark water. The scattered rays of the small central oil flame, bent into one narrow sheet of light by the angled glass prisms, were sent twenty miles out to sea by the revolving lens. Caleb tied on a soft linen apron so his coat buttons would not scratch the crystal.

Moving with steady care, Caleb dipped a lambskin cloth into a bowl of whiting powder and wiped each curved prism from left to right. Halfway around the frame, his fingers felt a gritty crust near the upper vent. A sharp gust during the morning squall had blown fine beach sand through a tiny gap in the brass shutter. Caleb paused and reached for his camel-hair brush instead of rubbing the sand with his cloth.

He knew that pressing down on sharp grains of quartz would carve permanent scratches into the soft French glass. Gently, he whisked every speck of grit into his palm before touching the linen cloth to the surface. His arms ached from reaching high above his head, and the rising wind hummed against the iron roof. Still, he checked each ring twice until the glass shone like clear ice.

Just as dusk settled over the tossing waves, his father's boots clanged up the iron stairs. Together they trimmed the cotton wick and struck a match. Instant beams of golden light pierced the driving rain and swept across the dark channel. Down near the outer sandbar, a wooden schooner flashed its deck lantern in thanks, guided safely home by the spotless glass.

tier2Words.definition: a very strong windstorm, especially along the coast
tier2Words.rootHint: From early English gale, referring to a fierce sea wind
tier2Words.contextClue: Gray clouds rolled low across the sound while stiff gusts of wind rattled the brass latches and drove white foam.

tier2Words.definition: a bright guiding light placed in a high spot to warn or direct ships
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English beacen, meaning 'sign or signal light'
tier2Words.contextClue: Even a thin film of soot could dim the lighthouse light's reach across the dark water.

tier2Words.definition: turning around a central point in a steady circle
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root volvere ('to roll or turn') + prefix re- ('back, again')
tier2Words.contextClue: As the lens turned in the lantern room, beams of golden light swept across the dark channel.

tier2Words.definition: lasting forever without fading or going away
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root manere ('to remain') + prefix per- ('completely')
tier2Words.contextClue: Pressing sharp grains of sand against the soft glass would carve lasting scratches that could never be wiped off.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The scattered rays of the small central oil flame, bent into one narrow sheet of light by the angled glass prisms, were sent twenty miles out to sea by the revolving lens."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what bends the scattered rays into a narrow sheet, and what sends them out to sea?

options.text: The angled glass prisms bend the rays into a narrow sheet, and the revolving lens sends them out to sea.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrases 'bent... by the angled glass prisms' and 'were sent... by the revolving lens' show that the glass prisms bend the light rays and the revolving lens sends them out to sea.

options.text: The small oil flame bends the revolving lens, and the sea sends the glass prisms twenty miles away.
options.childFeedback: This scrambles the parts of the sentence! The small oil flame makes the light rays, the glass prisms bend them, and the revolving lens sends the light out to sea.

options.text: Caleb's linen apron bends the light rays, and the brass window latches send them across the marsh.
options.childFeedback: Caleb wears his soft linen apron to avoid scratching the crystal, and the brass window latches just rattle in the wind.

options.text: A passing wooden schooner shines its deck lantern into the tower to light the oil wick.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, the wooden schooner flashes its deck lantern in thanks after seeing the lighthouse beam—it does not light the oil wick inside the tower.

questions.provingSentenceText: The scattered rays of the small central oil flame, bent into one narrow sheet of light by the angled glass prisms, were sent twenty miles out to sea by the revolving lens.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrases 'bent... by the angled glass prisms' and 'were sent... by the revolving lens' show that the glass prisms bend the light rays and the revolving lens sends them out to sea.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive sentence contains two 'by' phrases: 'bent... by the angled glass prisms' and 'were sent... by the revolving lens'. Option B accurately tracks both agents.
questions.retryHint: Look at the two 'by' phrases in Paragraph 2: 'bent... by...' and 'were sent... by...'

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"He knew that pressing down on sharp grains of quartz would carve permanent scratches into the soft French glass."

What does the word permanent mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: Easy to wash off with warm water and soap
options.childFeedback: If scratches were easy to wash off with warm water and soap, Caleb would not need to whisk away every grain of sand so carefully first.

options.text: Lasting forever and impossible to wipe away
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'permanent' means lasting forever and impossible to wipe away, because pressing down on sharp quartz sand would carve lasting scratches into the soft French glass.

options.text: Glowing brightly like a golden oil flame
options.childFeedback: The oil flame glows brightly in Paragraph 5, whereas 'permanent scratches' in Paragraph 4 describes damage carved into the glass surface.

options.text: Hidden underneath the spiral iron staircase
options.childFeedback: The spiral iron staircase is what Caleb climbs in Paragraph 1; 'permanent' describes scratches that would stay in the glass rings forever.

questions.provingSentenceText: He knew that pressing down on sharp grains of quartz would carve permanent scratches into the soft French glass.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'permanent' means lasting forever and impossible to wipe away, because pressing down on sharp quartz sand would carve lasting scratches into the soft French glass.
questions.parentExplanation: Because sharp sand grains would 'carve' scratches into the soft French glass if rubbed, 'permanent' means lasting or irreversible damage.
questions.retryHint: Think about why Caleb carefully whisks every speck of sand away with a brush before rubbing the soft glass in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, why does Caleb tie on a soft linen apron before he begins cleaning the lens?

options.text: He uses the apron to block the broken window shutter so rain cannot enter.
options.childFeedback: Caleb wears the linen apron over his coat while cleaning the lens; he never stuffs the apron into the brass window shutter.

options.text: He needs a heavy coat to stay warm while walking into the village for lamp oil.
options.childFeedback: Caleb's father is the one who rode into the village for lamp oil in Paragraph 1, and a thin linen apron is for protecting the glass, not staying warm outdoors.

options.text: He wants to keep the hard buttons on his coat from scratching the glass rings.
options.childFeedback: The last sentence of Paragraph 2 states that Caleb tied on a soft linen apron so the hard buttons on his coat would not scratch the polished crystal lens.

options.text: He is required to wear a white uniform whenever a ship passes the island.
options.childFeedback: Passing ships out at sea cannot see what Caleb is wearing inside the lantern room; the apron is strictly to protect the crystal from button scratches.

questions.provingSentenceText: Caleb tied on a soft linen apron so his coat buttons would not scratch the crystal.
questions.childTip: The last sentence of Paragraph 2 states that Caleb tied on a soft linen apron so the hard buttons on his coat would not scratch the polished crystal lens.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that Caleb tied on a soft linen apron 'so his coat buttons would not scratch the crystal.'
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 2 to see what Caleb's coat buttons might do to the crystal without an apron.

questions.prompt: How does Paragraph 1 contribute to the plot of the story?

options.text: It explains how French scientists invented the first beehive lens in Europe.
options.childFeedback: The French glass is mentioned briefly in Paragraph 4, and Paragraph 1 never explains the history of how scientists invented the lens in Europe.

options.text: It proves that Caleb prefers working in the village store over climbing lighthouse stairs.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 never says Caleb prefers working in a village store; he climbs the lighthouse steps ready to handle the important chore his father trusted him with.

options.text: It shows the wooden schooner flashing its deck lantern near the outer sandbar.
options.childFeedback: The wooden schooner does not appear near the outer sandbar until the end of the story in Paragraph 5, after the lamp is lit at dusk.

options.text: It establishes the stormy coastal setting and explains why Caleb is responsible for preparing the lens alone.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 sets up the approaching coastal storm on St. Simons Island and explains that Caleb's father rode to the village for oil, leaving Caleb in charge of the crucial afternoon chore.

questions.provingSentenceText: Before leaving, he had trusted Caleb with the afternoon chore that mattered most to passing ships.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 sets up the approaching coastal storm on St. Simons Island and explains that Caleb's father rode to the village for oil, leaving Caleb in charge of the crucial afternoon chore.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the historical setting (St. Simons Island, 1898), the rising storm, and the conflict/duty placed on Caleb while his father fetches oil.
questions.retryHint: Look at the weather details and the reason Caleb's father left in Paragraph 1.

questions.prompt: Part A: What can the reader infer about Caleb from the way he handles the gritty sand in Paragraphs 3 and 4?

options.text: He is a well-trained and conscientious worker who takes time to protect delicate equipment even when tired.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraphs 3 and 4, when Caleb feels gritty beach sand on the prism, he pauses, uses a soft camel-hair brush to whisk every speck away, and checks each ring twice despite his aching arms.

options.text: He is afraid of heights and rushes through his chores so he can climb back down the stairs.
options.childFeedback: Instead of rushing down the stairs, Caleb slows down to brush away every grain of sand and checks each glass ring twice until his father arrives.

options.text: He forgets his father's instructions and accidentally scratches the upper glass prism with his cloth.
options.childFeedback: Caleb remembers that quartz sand would scratch the soft glass, so he stops before rubbing it with his cloth and keeps the lens spotless.

options.text: He believes that a few smudges of soot and sand make no difference to the brightness of the lamp.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 states the exact opposite: even a thin film of soot or smudge of salt dust could dim the beacon's reach across the dark water.

questions.provingSentenceText: Gently, he whisked every speck of grit into his palm before touching the linen cloth to the surface.
questions.childTip: In Paragraphs 3 and 4, when Caleb feels gritty beach sand on the prism, he pauses, uses a soft camel-hair brush to whisk every speck away, and checks each ring twice despite his aching arms.
questions.parentExplanation: Caleb recognizes the danger of rubbing quartz sand against soft French glass, switches tools to whisk the grit away first, and double-checks every ring even when his arms ache.
questions.retryHint: Look at how Caleb switches to his camel-hair brush in Paragraph 3 and checks each ring twice in Paragraph 4.
